description: "How NCodeGroup code keeps request paths bounded and cheap: caching and failure caching of remote fetches, bounded caches, batched and paged store access, allocation-free hot paths, benchmark practice for primitives, and front-end load behaviour."
applyTo: "**/*.cs, **/*.csproj, **/Directory.Build.props, **/*.ts, **/*.tsx, **/*.ps1, **/*.psm1, **/.github/workflows/**"

# Performance

<!-- Generated by `npm run train` from the sources each rule cites. To change a rule for good, change its source or say so in training/feedback.md; the next training run regenerates this file. -->

- **Bound every in-memory cache. Build its keys from registration or configuration values, not from request input. If the keys have to come from tenant- or caller-controlled values, give the cache a size limit or an idle expiry that disposes entries, so it can't grow for the life of the process.** If callers or tenants control how many distinct keys exist, they control how much memory, how many connection pools and how many background refreshes the process holds. *Check:* Look for caches or long-lived dictionaries whose keys come from query strings, headers, route values, body fields or tenant identities, and that have no size limit or expiry and are cleared only on Dispose. *Note:* Where a cache's keys are per server by specification, as with DPoP nonces (RFC 9449 §8), key it by origin (scheme, host and port), not by the full URI, and clear it when it reaches its fixed size limit. <sub>Identity ADR-1381; Identity outcomes of #584; Identity ADR-1286</sub>
- **Don't report a per-replica cache in a singleton as unbounded, or as a breach of the stateless-singleton rule, when its keys come only from configuration, a miss only causes the value to be recomputed, and a decision record accepts it as an exception.** Such a cache holds at most one entry per configured key, and a replica that misses or restarts just recomputes the value. *Check:* Before reporting, trace where the keys come from, confirm that a miss only causes a recomputation, and look for the decision record. <sub>Identity outcomes of #520</sub>
- **Fetch a shared remote resource (a metadata document, a key set, a revocation list, a caller-supplied URL) once for all concurrent callers, for example through a `ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, Lazy<Task<T>>>` entry that removes itself. Bound the fetch by its own timeout, not by one caller's `CancellationToken`; callers wait on it with `WaitAsync`.** Without this, each concurrent miss or request starts its own outbound fetch, and a caller that cancels would cancel the fetch for everyone else. *Check:* Look for shared resources fetched once per request or once per concurrent caller, and for shared fetches tied to a caller's token. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1285</sub>
- **Remember a failed shared or caller-triggered outbound fetch for a positive failure duration that is a configured option. The failure can be unreachable, non-2xx, oversized, malformed or refused content, or an empty result. Don't start a new fetch while the failure is remembered, and log each suppressed fetch at debug level.** Without failure caching, an unreachable endpoint costs the full timeout on every request, and a client that sends many requests makes the server send as many outbound fetches. The remembered failure is the back-off between attempts. *Check:* Look at outbound fetches. Report failures that aren't cached, a remembered failure that still lets a new fetch start, a hard-coded failure duration, and suppression that isn't logged. <sub>Identity ADR-1106; Identity ADR-1259; Identity ADR-1400; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **When a cache of remote metadata or key sets fails to refresh, serve the last good value only within a bounded stale lifetime and back off for a minimum interval. Rate-limit forced refreshes, such as one triggered by an unknown `kid`, with that same interval, and never relax validation to serve a stale value.** This limits the load on the provider and how long stale data can be served, and a stale value never gets around validation. *Check:* Look for stale values served with no age limit, forced refreshes with no rate limit, or validation skipped on the stale path. <sub>Identity ADR-1285</sub>
- **Never run work in a request that grows with the size of the data or the deployment, such as a pass over every record, tenant, client or team. In production code, run it as a paged background pass on one replica that reads lightweight projections, not as a job on a bounded in-process job dispatcher.** Such work makes request latency grow without limit, and on the dispatcher it ties up the bounded workers. *Check:* Look for full-table scans, loops over all entities or tenants in request handlers, unpaged reads of whole sets, and such passes queued on an in-process job dispatcher. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Page any list or on-demand report over a collection that can grow without limit. Normalize the limit to a default and a maximum, return a continuation token, and treat an empty page that still carries a token as not the end of the results.** The work done by one request must not grow with the size of the collection. *Check:* Look for list or report endpoints that compute over every item in one request, and for callers that stop at an empty page while the continuation token is still set. <sub>Identity ADR-1245</sub>
- **Walk a hierarchy whose fan-out has no limit depth first, reading one bounded page of children per level. Don't read every descendant of a node as one list.** A node can have any number of children, so a whole-subtree read or a breadth-first level can be arbitrarily large. A paged depth-first walk keeps memory to depth times page size. *Check:* Look for queries that return all descendants at once, and for breadth-first walks that hold a whole level in memory. <sub>Identity ADR-1426; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Have a reconciliation pass that follows a change read only the items the change can affect, by comparing the previous and current settings. Reconcile every item only when the previous state is missing or can't be read.** A small change must not read the whole deployment. *Check:* Look for reconciliation handlers that enumerate every tenant or item without filtering by what changed. <sub>Identity ADR-1412</sub>
- **Don't make one store call per id or per item inside a loop. Gather the keys and read them with a batched get-many query, once per request or once per page.** Per-item queries add a database round trip for every entity, and the number grows with the input. *Check:* Look for an awaited store call such as `GetOrDefaultAsync(id)` inside a `foreach` over ids or over the items of a page. <sub>Identity outcomes of #585; Identity outcomes of #599</sub>
- **Reuse data the method or the unit of work has already loaded instead of reading it from the store again. This covers a parent, a lineage, and entities the DbContext already tracks (check `DbSet<T>.Local` before querying in a load-then-update flow).** Reading data that is already in hand turns one read into many queries. *Check:* Look for loops that call a store-backed resolve or count method for each element of a collection that was just read, and for update flows that query again for an entity loaded earlier in the same unit of work. <sub>Identity outcomes of #599; Identity ADR-1012</sub>
- **Don't report per-level store round trips in a recursive cache-miss walk up a hierarchy that stops at the first cached ancestor, and don't propose reading the whole lineage first instead.** Such a walk usually reads only the missing leaf, and a lineage-first read costs more queries in that common case. *Check:* Confirm that the recursion returns at the first cache hit, and compare what the proposed bulk read would cost when only the leaf is missing. <sub>Identity outcomes of #599</sub>
- **Don't ask for keyed single-row lookups to be replaced by loading a whole collection into memory when the operation is an infrequent operator action and a decision record accepts how its cost grows.** Loading every row of a large tenant reads far more than the operation needs, while keyed single-row reads are cheap. *Check:* Check that each lookup is a keyed single-row read, how often the operation runs, and whether a decision record accepts the cost. <sub>Identity outcomes of #592</sub>
- **Don't await a sequence of remote round trips, such as one KMS unwrap per row, while holding a per-key lock or `SemaphoreSlim` on a request path. Limit the work to what the request needs, or move it outside the lock or into a background service.** The first request waits for N round trips, and every concurrent request for the same key queues behind it. *Check:* Look for loops of awaited remote calls inside a held lock or semaphore on a request path. <sub>Identity outcomes of #572</sub>
- **When several limits apply to one request, judge them in one batched, atomic call to the counter store that stops at the first limit exceeded. Don't make sequential round trips, pipeline the increments, or increment and compensate afterwards. Judge a quota and its overage allowance with one counter whose limit is the quota plus the allowance.** Sequential calls cost one round trip per limit. A pipeline can't stop at the first refusal, so a refused request still spends later allowances. Compensation leaves an over-count that refuses other callers until it runs, and a second overage counter adds state and round trips. *Check:* Look for loops that await one increment per limit, pipelined increments with no early stop, decrement-after-refusal logic, or a separate overage counter. <sub>Identity ADR-1246; Identity ADR-1198</sub>
- **Keep high-frequency side records, such as per-request usage accounting and records from audit or event handlers, off the request path. Count or enqueue them in memory, with the queue bounded, and have a hosted service write them to storage periodically in bounded batches.** A write per request puts log-level write load on the database, adds a round trip to every operation, and fails the operation when the write fails. *Check:* Look for handlers that call a store, `DbContext` or `SaveChanges` for usage or audit data inside the request, for unbounded queues, and for flush batches with no fixed maximum size. <sub>Identity ADR-1199; Identity ADR-1303</sub>
- **In production code, record usage through the rate-limit descriptor meters, not through a separate usage-recorder call next to a limit. Exclude public metadata endpoints that anonymous callers or caches fetch, such as discovery and JWKS, from tenant quotas and billable usage.** Recording usage separately double-counts requests or counts refused ones, and anonymous fetches shouldn't spend a tenant's quota. *Check:* Look for direct usage-record calls in endpoints, and for metadata endpoints that are still metered. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Answer a question that several places ask in one request once, and memoize the answer in `HttpContext.Items`. Store negative answers too, and don't read the store again for a key that has already been answered.** Repeated reads cost round trips, and a later reader, such as an audit recorder that runs after commit, can get a different answer once the data has changed. *Check:* Look for per-request resolvers that read the store again or open a new store manager on each call, or that memoize only positive answers. <sub>Identity ADR-1466</sub>
- **In a request handler, run a lookup whose result only feeds a later step, such as an audit record, after input validation has passed.** A lookup placed before validation adds a query to every request, including the ones that then fail validation. *Check:* Look for a store query that runs before a validate call even though its result is used only after validation succeeds. <sub>Identity outcomes of #839</sub>
- **In production code, don't repeat certificate verification work on every request. Cache the verdict per certificate, for example by thumbprint plus anchor generation, with an expiry no later than the end of the certificate's validity and a size limit. Parse configured values once, and check backing files for changes at most once per interval, outside any global lock.** Rebuilding an `X509Chain`, parsing options again and statting a file under a lock on every request adds system calls, allocations and lock contention to the hottest path, even though a keep-alive connection presents the same certificate each time. *Check:* Look for per-request middleware or verifiers that create an `X509Chain`, parse options, or call `File.GetLastWriteTimeUtc` inside a lock. Check that any verdict cache has a size limit and an expiry. <sub>Identity outcomes of #794</sub>
- **Slide a session's idle expiry only on real user activity, not on polling or status endpoints such as user-info, and write it only after a set fraction of the idle timeout has passed since the last write.** Otherwise polling keeps a session alive forever and a busy session writes to the store on every call. *Check:* Look for idle-expiry updates on every request, or on polling or status endpoints. <sub>Identity ADR-1290</sub>
- **Make a check that runs on every configuration change answer whether a resource exists without loading the resource, for example without reading key files or decoding keys.** Loading in the check reads every file on every change, and a load failure would refuse the configuration for a reason the name doesn't show. *Check:* Look for configuration-change validators that load keys or read files only to learn whether a name exists. <sub>Identity ADR-1439</sub>
- **Serve a JWKS or other public-key endpoint from cached public keys, not by calling the remote key management service on each request.** Each remote call adds a network round trip and costs money, and public keys are safe to cache. *Check:* Look for JWKS or public-key endpoints that call a KMS or vault client on every request with no cache. <sub>Identity docs/hosting-analysis.md</sub>
- **Keep caches of large, rebuildable data fetched over the network, and the remembered failures of those fetches, in the process-local `IMemoryCache`, not in a distributed or shared-state store.** The data is large and can be rebuilt, and a network failure on one replica must not stop the others. *Check:* Look for downloaded revocation lists, key sets or similar fetched data, or their failure entries, written to a distributed cache. <sub>Identity ADR-1400</sub>
- **Give each per-instance cache entry an absolute lifetime. After commit, announce changes as a best-effort hint that carries only the id; log a failed announcement without failing the write. Drop entries that may have been invalidated after a reconnect. Add eviction disposal only for entries that own native or disposable resources.** An absolute lifetime limits staleness without tying writes to messaging. Entries holding native handles leak without disposal, while plain data such as public keys needs no eviction callback. *Check:* Look for entries with only sliding expiration, data carried in invalidation messages, writes that fail on announcement errors, native-handle entries with no eviction disposal, and needless eviction callbacks on plain data. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1106</sub>
- **When a broadcast subscription reports that messages may have been missed, revalidate the cache instead of clearing it. Compare each entry's row concurrency token with the store's current token, and evict only the entries whose token differs or whose row no longer exists.** Clearing everything rebuilds every entry the replica serves, with all its store reads, mostly for changes that never happened. An equal token proves the cached copy is unchanged. *Check:* Look at missed-message handlers that clear every cache without comparing tokens, or that compare something other than the row's concurrency token. <sub>Identity ADR-1416</sub>
- **When a supplied secret is checked against several stored verifiers, try the verifiers with no work factor before any work-factor (KDF) verifier.** In storage order, a wrong secret costs one full key derivation per stored verifier, which uses up gate capacity and slows legitimate requests. *Check:* Look for verifier loops that run KDF-based verifiers before fast-hash ones. <sub>Identity ADR-1391; Identity outcomes of #531</sub>
- **When a token header's `kid` matches eligible decryption keys, try only those keys, not every candidate key.** A token that names its key then costs at most one key-service call per matching key. *Check:* Look at decryption key selection loops that fall back to all keys even when a `kid` matches. <sub>Identity ADR-1472</sub>
- **Serve content-hashed static assets with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` plus `ETag`, `Last-Modified` and range support, and send no cache lifetime on a `404`. In production code, serve them from a file provider rooted at the assets folder, so nothing outside it (`index.html` included) can be served, and from a route group that does no tenant resolution and runs no tenant filters.** A hashed file never changes under its name, but validators alone make the browser revalidate on every use. Tenant resolution adds work and makes an unknown tenant's assets return `404`, and rooting the provider limits what can be exposed. *Check:* Look for hashed-asset handlers without the immutable one-year header or the validators, a cache lifetime on not-found responses, file providers rooted above the assets folder, and asset routes that resolve the tenant. <sub>Identity ADR-1193; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Cache a parsed build artifact, such as a bundle's index file, keyed by its file version (last-write time and length), and revalidate that metadata on each request. Don't parse it on every request, and don't invalidate it with a file watcher.** The file changes once per build. A watcher holds an operating-system handle for the life of the host and behaves differently on different container file systems. *Check:* Look for per-request reads or parses of a static index file, and for `FileSystemWatcher` or `IFileProvider.Watch` used to invalidate the cache. <sub>Identity ADR-1193</sub>
- **Return a buffered collection by default. Return a lazy `IEnumerable<T>` or `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` only for a sequence that is large, unbounded, backed by I/O or usually short-circuited, and never for one that captures request state or that callers enumerate twice or count. An interface method that lists a large, paged remote or database set streams it as `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`.** A lazy sequence repeats its work on each enumeration and can outlive the state it captures, while materializing an unbounded remote listing holds all of it in memory. *Check:* Look for `yield return` or deferred LINQ returned from methods that capture request state or whose results are enumerated more than once, and for new interface methods that return `Task<List<T>>` or arrays for unbounded remote listings. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1478</sub>
- **On per-request paths in production code, use `foreach` loops instead of LINQ (`Any`, `Where`, `Select`, `ToList`, `ToDictionary`, `Distinct`, `OrderBy`) and instead of `string.Split`. Parse header and query values over spans with `MemoryExtensions.Split` into a `Range` buffer. Normalize a small set by copying it into one array, sorting it in place with `Array.Sort` and an ordinal comparer, and removing adjacent duplicates. Build collections into named locals rather than inline in arguments.** LINQ and `string.Split` allocate delegates, enumerators, sort buffers and substring arrays on every request. *Check:* Look for LINQ calls, `[.. x.Select(...)]` spreads or `Split(` in middleware, handlers and other code that runs on each request or page render. *Note:* The 'Don't report a small per-call allocation' rule limits this one: don't report single allocations that can't be measured next to much larger per-call work. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #547; Identity outcomes of #548; Identity outcomes of #839</sub>
- **Create a `List<T>`, `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` or `HashSet<T>` with an initial capacity when the number of entries is known up front. Return a shared empty instance, such as `FrozenDictionary<TKey,TValue>.Empty` or `Array.Empty<T>()`, instead of a new empty collection. In production code on per-call paths, test `Count == 0` before a `foreach` over an interface-typed collection.** A collection without its known capacity resizes while it is filled, a new empty collection allocates on every read, and a `foreach` over an interface allocates a boxed enumerator even when the collection is empty. *Check:* Look for collections filled from a source whose `Count` is available but created without that capacity, new empty collections returned for empty input, and `foreach` over `IReadOnlyList`/`ICollection` on hot paths with no empty check. <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #554; Identity outcomes of #577; Identity outcomes of #839</sub>
- **Don't remove elements one at a time with `RemoveAt` inside a loop over a list or `JsonArray` whose size comes from input. Build the result in one pass into a pre-sized list.** Each `RemoveAt` shifts every later element, so a large input costs quadratic time. *Check:* Look for `RemoveAt(index)` inside a loop over a collection whose size comes from input. <sub>Identity outcomes of #552</sub>
- **In production code on hot paths, transform identifiers into rented `char` spans, for example with `MemoryExtensions.ToLowerInvariant(source, destination)`, instead of allocating new strings. Build per-element strings, such as JSON Pointer paths, only for the elements or error paths that use them.** Per-request string allocations add up, and building a path for every member allocates one string per member on every request, with strings that grow with depth. *Check:* Look for `string.ToLowerInvariant()`/`ToUpperInvariant()` on per-request paths, and for path or label strings built for every member of a walk when only some members use them. <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #552</sub>
- **When the same hash function runs on several values with the same output size one after another, allocate the output buffer once in the caller and pass it to each call. If that needs a `Span<byte>` inside an async method, move the work into a synchronous helper.** Reusing one buffer avoids repeated allocations. Dropping this reuse was a performance regression. *Check:* Look for consecutive hash computations, such as `at_hash`, `c_hash` and `s_hash`, where each call allocates or stackallocs its own buffer of the same size. <sub>Identity review of #341</sub>
- **Don't change one member of a JSON document by round-tripping it through text and several representations (string to `JsonNode` to string to `JsonElement`). Build the modified copy in one pass with a dedicated helper, for example one that uses `Utf8JsonWriter`, and remove the error branches that become unreachable.** The round trips allocate more and create a second construction path that has to be kept in step with the first. A `JsonObject` built from untrusted JSON can also throw on duplicate members. *Check:* Look for chains of `ToJsonString`/`JsonNode.Parse`/`JsonElement.Parse` used to add or replace one property, and for error branches after the input has already been validated. <sub>Identity outcomes of #757</sub>
- **When a `ValueTask`-returning method usually finishes synchronously, return a completed `ValueTask` (`new ValueTask<T>(result)` or `ValueTask.FromResult`) on that path without an async state machine, and await only on the path that is really asynchronous.** The common synchronous case, such as signing with a local key, then pays no allocation for the async seam. *Check:* Look for `async` methods whose synchronous branch still goes through the state machine. <sub>Identity ADR-1472</sub>
- **Don't report readability problems in the inner loops of cryptographic or numeric primitives that use aggressive optimization (`AggressiveInlining`/`AggressiveOptimization`, manual unrolling, `stackalloc`, `MemoryMarshal`/`Unsafe` reinterpretation). Do report an optimization that adds a branch or memory access that depends on secret data to constant-time code, or that has no passing test vectors.** These primitives put speed ahead of readability, but they never give up constant-time behaviour or correctness that test vectors pin down. *Check:* In changes to math or crypto primitives, look for branches or indexing that depend on secret values, and for missing test vectors. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Back an optimization of a hot-path primitive (field, scalar or group arithmetic, encoders, constant-time helpers) with a benchmark in the benchmark projects. The pull request quotes before and after BenchmarkDotNet tables run in Release on the same developer machine. Never quote numbers from CI, and never run benchmarks in CI or gate on them.** An optimization of a hot primitive needs measured evidence, and shared CI runners give numbers too noisy to prove anything. *Check:* Look for micro-optimizations of primitives with no benchmark added or updated, or with no before and after tables from one machine in the description, and for workflow steps that run benchmarks or gate on them. <sub>Identity ADR-1266; Identity ADR-1386; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **When code reinterprets a struct's fields as contiguous memory, for example with `Unsafe.As` or `MemoryMarshal.Cast`, declare the struct with an explicit `[StructLayout(LayoutKind.Sequential)]` or another explicit layout. For tiny fixed-limb structs in arithmetic code, prefer direct field access to a span view.** The reinterpreting code depends on the field layout, and the attribute records that layout as a contract. Direct field access is faster than a span view over a struct this small. *Check:* Find `Unsafe.As<TStruct, T>`, `MemoryMarshal.Cast` or similar over a struct's fields and check that the struct has a `[StructLayout]` attribute. Look for span views over small fixed-limb structs in arithmetic code. <sub>Identity ADR-1486; Identity ADR-1266</sub>
- **Make a benchmark class `public`, unsealed and marked `[MemoryDiagnoser]`, and take its inputs from a `Random` with a fixed seed. Keep an input that the measured method takes by `in` or fills by `out` in a private field, and store a result of an `internal` type in a private auto-property instead of returning it from the public benchmark method.** BenchmarkDotNet derives from the class, the diagnoser reports allocations, and a fixed seed gives the same inputs on every run. A ref target can't be a property, and a public method can't return an `internal` type. *Check:* In benchmark projects, look for sealed or non-public benchmark classes, a missing `[MemoryDiagnoser]`, unseeded or nondeterministic inputs, benchmark methods that return internal types, and `in`/`out` inputs held in properties. Don't report private ref-target fields in a benchmark class as breaking the field-to-property rule. <sub>Identity ADR-1386</sub>
- **Have a benchmark project's `Main` inspect the BenchmarkDotNet summaries and return exit code 1 when any benchmark fails.** A `--job Dry` run then works as a smoke check. A run that ignores failures can't be used as one. *Check:* Look at the benchmark `Program.cs` for a `Main` that ignores failed summaries. <sub>Identity ADR-1386</sub>
- **Keep the Request Delegate Generator turned on through one family-wide switch in `Directory.Build.props`. Opt a project out (`EnableRequestDelegateGenerator=false`) only if it has a form-bound endpoint.** Generated delegates remove the expression-tree compilation and JIT of every endpoint from each host start, which speeds up integration suites and production cold starts. *Check:* Look for a `.csproj` that disables the generator without having a form-bound endpoint, and for a change that removes the family-wide switch. <sub>Identity ADR-1262</sub>
- **Don't report one small per-call allocation or parse, such as a `Uri` parse or an `AsyncLocal` restore scope, on a path that already does much more work (an HTTP round trip, per-invocation framework work) unless a measurement shows it matters.** The cost can't be measured next to the surrounding work, and caching it would add state to transient types. *Check:* Before reporting, weigh the per-call cost of the surrounding work, check whether the work is needed for correctness on every call, and look for a measurement. <sub>Identity outcomes of #600</sub>
- **Don't report creating a new `HttpMessageInvoker` per request around `IHttpMessageHandlerFactory.CreateHandler` as a per-request handler allocation, and don't ask for the invoker to be cached.** `CreateHandler` returns the cached handler of the name's active entry, so the only per-request cost is a small invoker. Caching the invoker would break the handler rotation that the factory owns. *Check:* Confirm that the handler comes from `IHttpMessageHandlerFactory` and that the invoker doesn't own it (for example, `disposeHandler: false`). <sub>Identity outcomes of #722</sub>
- **Don't report that per-key AWS KMS metadata calls (`ListResourceTags`, `DescribeKey`) made by an infrequent background sweep will throttle live cryptographic traffic.** AWS KMS counts these calls against quotas separate from the cryptographic-operation quota, so a sequential sweep can't throttle Sign or Decrypt. *Check:* Before reporting a throttling risk, check which KMS quota the calls fall under and how often the sweep runs. <sub>Identity outcomes of #702</sub>
- **Don't report collections on one-shot input parameter objects, or on result types built only internally from new collections, as needing to be frozen or copied.** No caller holds a mutable reference to them, so freezing them would cost a copy and protect nothing. *Check:* Before reporting unowned collections, check whether the type is a one-shot input or is built only by internal code from new collections. <sub>Identity outcomes of #554</sub>
- **Don't ask for a background or concurrent call to be skipped up front just because its result looks predictable, when the called function makes its own early checks that the skip condition would have to copy and starting it costs little next to the work it overlaps.** Skipping it up front copies the function's decision logic into a second place that has to stay in step, to save a few milliseconds. *Check:* Before reporting, read the called function to confirm that its answer really is known before it runs on that path, and compare its start-up cost with the work it runs alongside. <sub>project-template outcomes of #183</sub>
- **When a client bundle replaces a server-rendered page, mount it at once from data the server embedded in that page. Don't fetch data the host already knows before mounting, and don't theme the page again when a later fetch returns.** While the bundle waits on the network, the user's typed or autofilled input, focus and cleared choices are lost when the page is replaced. A late reply themes the page a second time. *Check:* In mount or bootstrap code, look for a network request (fetch, a query hook) that runs before `createRoot(...).render`, or a re-theme after the first render, for data the server could have embedded. <sub>Identity ADR-1253</sub>
- **Load route-level containers with `React.lazy` inside a `Suspense` boundary. Tests that assert on a lazily loaded container wait for it with `findBy...` queries.** The shell paints before a route's code arrives, and a route that is never visited is never downloaded. A synchronous `getBy` or `queryBy` query runs before the lazy chunk has resolved. *Check:* Look for static imports of route-level containers in app shells, and for tests that use `getBy` or `queryBy` against lazily loaded content. <sub>Identity ADR-1151</sub>
